title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array: slow/fast pointer.
shortTitle: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array: Slow/Fast Pointer In Place
keyPoints: A slow write pointer plus a fast scan pointer compacts a sorted array to its unique values in one pass with O(1) extra space.
The slow pointer k marks where the next unique value belongs; the fast pointer i scans every element.
When a[i] differs from a[k], advance k and copy a[i] to a[k].
The method returns k + 1 as the count of unique elements; the first k + 1 slots hold them in order.
This works because the array is sorted, so all copies of a value are contiguous.
Java arrays cannot shrink, so the caller must treat only the returned prefix as valid.
Generalizes to 'allow at most 2 copies' by comparing against a[k-1] instead of a[k].

s1_definition.oneliner: A slow write pointer plus a fast scan pointer compacts a sorted array to its unique values in one pass with no extra memory.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Same-direction two pointers** – a slow pointer `k` marks where the next unique value should be written; a fast pointer `i` scans every element.
- **Copy-on-new rule** – when `a[i] != a[k]`, increment `k` and copy `a[i]` to `a[k]`.
- **Return value** – `k + 1` is the count of unique elements; the first `k + 1` slots hold them in sorted order.
- **O(n) time, O(1) space** – one pass through the array with only an index variable as extra state.
- **Sorted precondition** – duplicates must be contiguous for the comparison to catch every group.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh at the National Bank of India has a sorted printout of account numbers where some appear more than once because of repeated statement imports. He keeps one finger on the slot where the next fresh number should go and scans ahead with another finger. Each time he sees a number different from the last kept one, he writes it into the fresh slot and moves on. He compacts the list without a second sheet of paper.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Removing duplicates from a sorted array in place is a same-direction two-pointer problem. You keep a slow pointer that marks the slot where the next unique value should be written, and a fast pointer that scans every element. The first element is always unique so the slow pointer starts there, and whenever the fast pointer finds a value different from the one at the slow pointer, you advance the slow pointer and copy the new value. The slow pointer plus one gives the count of unique values, compacted at the front.

The reason this works is that the array is sorted, so all copies of a value are next to each other, which means you only need to compare the current element against the last value you kept rather than against everything. On unsorted data this breaks because duplicates are scattered, and you would need a HashSet at O(n) space cost.

A practical detail is that Java arrays cannot shrink, so the method returns the logical length and the caller must treat only that prefix as valid. In production, copy the prefix into a right-sized collection before passing it downstream.

In a banking project at the National Bank of India, the nightly ledger batch merges imports into one sorted file of transaction IDs, and because of retry logic the same ID can appear several times. Deduplicating in place keeps memory low on an already loaded batch server.

Remember one sentence: A slow write pointer and a fast scan pointer compact a sorted array to unique values in O(n) time and O(1) space.
